spec.cue: Three kinds of colour sensor in many species, a sharp middle, and eyes that dart about.

M.note: the three peaks sit near marmoset, owl monkey and cynomolgus records; the mapping is the app's

cpd.note: the stumptail macaque figure, converted from 1.4 arc minutes; the app takes this one animal's value as its picture of sharpness

fovea.note: the app's choice of sharp-middle scale; no record gives a fovea scale for these animals

fov.note: no whole-field measurement was found; a person's width is used

gain.note: no dim-light ratio was found for these animals

rate.note: no flicker figure was taken for these animals

primate_trichro.note: peaks near the marmoset, owl monkey and cynomolgus records; the mapping is the app's

rows: Many monkeys and apes see three kinds of colour sensor; some New World species have only two, and owl monkeys see no colour at all.

A stumptail macaque with normal eyes resolves about 21 cycles per degree, close to a person's figure. A marmoset's fovea is estimated to resolve about 30. We blur the picture to about 21, the stumptail's figure.
Monkeys make small, quick eye movements even while they fix, averaging about half a degree. Microsaccades in rhesus monkeys average about 29 minutes of arc.
The sharp middle, the field width, the gain, the saturation, the frame rate and the picture's colour mapping are the app's choices, since no record gave them for these animals.

claims.how: The stumptail macaque's 1.4 arc minutes converts to 21.4 cycles per degree by 1 / (2 x 1.4/60), so the value is the record's converted figure.

quotes.quote: Visual acuity in a normal stumptail macaque is 1.4 minutes of arc-similar to man's.
The foveal acuity predicted by the Nyquist limits set by the cone mosaic (30 c/deg) is in agreement with behavioral measures of visual acuity.
The spatial resolution of the photoreceptor mosaic in the marmoset is therefore estimated to be close to 30 cycles/degree
